1. Project Idea

The project is an AI-powered personal career coaching and job-readiness platform designed to help students, fresh graduates, and early-career professionals move from “I want this job” to “I know exactly what I need to do to become ready for this job.” The core idea is to create a personalized career companion that understands a user's resume, skills, projects, education, experience, career goals, and target job requirements, and then continuously guides the user through the gap between their current profile and the profile expected by their desired role. Instead of functioning like a generic AI chatbot where a user has to repeatedly ask questions such as “Is my resume good?”, “What skills should I learn?”, “Am I suitable for this job?”, or “What questions should I prepare for?”, the platform connects all of these activities into one intelligent workflow. A user begins by creating a career profile and uploading their resume, after which the system extracts and analyzes the information contained in the resume to create a structured understanding of the user's current capabilities, including technical skills, soft skills, projects, technologies, education, experience, achievements, and areas that may require improvement. The user can then add a specific target job by pasting a job description or entering information about a role they are interested in. The platform analyzes the job description and identifies the important requirements, expected technologies, responsibilities, experience requirements, qualifications, and preferred skills associated with that role. These two pieces of information—the user's current profile and the requirements of the target job—are then intelligently compared to identify what the user already possesses, what is missing, what is partially demonstrated, which parts of their existing experience are relevant, and which areas deserve attention before applying or appearing for an interview. The result is not intended to be just a static “match score”; instead, the platform converts the comparison into meaningful, explainable, and actionable guidance. If a job requires React, Node.js, MongoDB, Docker, and AWS and the user's profile already demonstrates React, Node.js, and MongoDB but does not demonstrate Docker or AWS, the system should clearly explain the gap and recommend practical next steps rather than simply telling the user that two skills are missing. Based on this analysis, the platform generates a personalized career roadmap containing learning goals, practical tasks, project recommendations, preparation milestones, and interview topics that are relevant to the user's target role and current level. The roadmap can evolve as the user completes tasks, adds new skills, updates their resume, or changes their target role. The platform also includes an AI-powered interview preparation experience in which interview questions are generated based on the user's target role, job description, resume, projects, and previously identified skill gaps. Instead of asking only generic interview questions, the system can ask questions about technologies mentioned in the target job, projects actually present in the user's resume, and areas where the user needs additional preparation. After the user answers, the AI evaluates the response and provides structured feedback about correctness, completeness, technical depth, communication, and areas for improvement. The broader vision is therefore to create a single connected career workflow in which resume analysis, job analysis, skill-gap identification, learning guidance, interview preparation, and career progress are not separate tools but parts of one continuous system.

2. Product Overview

The product, currently referred to as CareerPilot, will be a web-based AI career coaching platform built around a structured, agent-driven workflow. The primary users will be students, fresh graduates, internship seekers, and early-career professionals who have difficulty understanding how their current skills and experience relate to the requirements of real-world job opportunities. CareerPilot will provide these users with a personalized workspace where they can maintain their career profile, upload and analyze their resume, define target roles, evaluate individual job opportunities, identify skill gaps, generate personalized preparation plans, practice interviews, and monitor their progress over time. The product will use a conventional full-stack web architecture for authentication, data storage, file management, dashboards, user profiles, and application management, while the intelligent reasoning layer will be powered by the Lemma SDK. Lemma will not simply be exposed as a standalone chatbot; instead, it will be incorporated into specialized AI workflows responsible for different parts of the career journey. A Resume Analysis Agent will transform an uploaded resume into structured career information; a Job Analysis Agent will convert an unstructured job description into structured requirements; a Matching and Skill-Gap Agent will compare the two profiles and identify similarities, missing requirements, partial matches, and relevant experience; a Career Planning Agent will use these findings to create a personalized action plan; and an Interview Coach Agent will use the user's target role, resume, job requirements, and skill gaps to generate and evaluate realistic interview practice. This separation of responsibilities is important because the product is intended to behave like a career system rather than a simple question-and-answer interface. The AI should retain meaningful career context throughout the user's journey so that the user does not need to repeatedly explain their background every time they want assistance.

The first experience will begin with a simple onboarding flow in which the user creates an account and provides basic information such as their current experience level, target career direction, and professional interests. The user will then upload a resume, preferably in PDF format, and the platform will process the document to extract its relevant textual information. The extracted information will be passed through the resume-analysis workflow, where the AI will identify and structure the user's education, technical skills, programming languages, frameworks, tools, projects, internship or work experience, achievements, certifications, and other relevant career information. This information will form the user's internal career profile and will be stored in the application's database so it can be reused throughout subsequent workflows. The platform should distinguish between information directly extracted from the user's resume and AI-generated interpretations or recommendations, ensuring that the user can understand what information came from their original document and what conclusions were produced by the AI.

Once a career profile has been created, the user can select a target role or evaluate a specific job opportunity. The user can paste a job description into the platform, and the Job Analysis workflow will break the unstructured description into meaningful categories such as job title, required technical skills, preferred skills, responsibilities, experience expectations, educational requirements, tools, frameworks, and other relevant qualifications. This structured job profile will then be compared against the user's existing career profile. The matching workflow will identify skills and requirements that are clearly demonstrated by the user's profile, requirements that appear to be missing, requirements that are only partially demonstrated, and existing projects or experiences that could be relevant to the position. Rather than reducing the entire analysis to a single opaque percentage, CareerPilot will provide an explainable breakdown that allows the user to understand exactly why a particular requirement is considered a match or a gap. For example, if a target position requires React, Node.js, MongoDB, AWS, Docker, and REST APIs, while the user's resume demonstrates React, Node.js, MongoDB, and REST APIs but contains no evidence of AWS or Docker, the platform can identify AWS and Docker as areas requiring attention and explain how those skills relate to the target position.

The most important part of the product is what happens after the gap analysis. CareerPilot should not stop at identifying weaknesses; it should turn those findings into a practical action plan. The Career Planning workflow will consider the user's current skill level, target role, identified gaps, available experience, and potentially the user's preferred preparation timeline to generate a personalized roadmap. The roadmap may contain learning topics, practical implementation tasks, project-based exercises, revision goals, interview preparation milestones, and progress checkpoints. For example, if the system identifies Docker as a missing skill for a Full Stack Developer role, it can recommend learning Docker fundamentals and then applying that knowledge by containerizing an existing project rather than simply telling the user to “learn Docker.” Similarly, if AWS is identified as a requirement, the roadmap can guide the user toward learning the relevant fundamentals and deploying a practical project. Every roadmap item should be trackable so that users can mark tasks as completed and see their progress toward their target role. The system can later use completed tasks and updated profile information to refresh the user's career analysis, making the experience iterative rather than one-time.

CareerPilot will also contain a dedicated AI Interview Coach designed to bridge the gap between learning and actual interview readiness. When a user begins an interview session, the system will use contextual information already available in the platform—including the user's target role, selected job description, resume, projects, technical skills, and identified gaps—to generate relevant questions. This means that a user who has listed a MERN project on their resume could receive questions about why MongoDB was chosen, how the Express APIs were structured, how authentication was implemented, what scalability challenges might occur, or how the project could be deployed. Similarly, if the target job requires React and the skill-gap analysis indicates that the user's React knowledge needs improvement, the interview coach can prioritize React-related questions. After the user submits an answer, the AI can evaluate it and provide structured feedback describing what was correct, what was incomplete, what concepts should be explained more clearly, and how the answer could be improved. Over multiple sessions, the platform can maintain an interview history so the user can observe which topics they repeatedly struggle with and use that information to adjust their preparation roadmap.

The product can also include a job application tracking layer so that the user's preparation is connected to actual job-search activity. Users can save relevant opportunities, record companies and positions, maintain application statuses, store job descriptions, and track stages such as saved, applied, assessment, interview, offer, or rejected. Because the job description is stored alongside the application, the platform can continue using that information for preparation. For example, before an interview, the user could open a particular application and immediately access the relevant job requirements, previously identified skill gaps, recommended preparation topics, and role-specific interview questions. This creates a continuous loop where the same information collected during the job-search process becomes useful for preparation rather than being stored as disconnected data.

From a technical perspective, CareerPilot will be implemented as a full-stack web application. The frontend will provide the dashboard, onboarding experience, resume upload interface, job-analysis interface, skill-gap visualizations, career roadmap, interview environment, and application tracker. The backend will manage authentication, user data, resume processing, job data, career plans, interview sessions, application records, API security, and communication with the AI layer. MongoDB can be used to persist user profiles, structured resume analyses, job descriptions, matching results, career plans, interview sessions, and application data. The Lemma SDK will form the intelligent orchestration layer responsible for the specialized AI workflows. The system should be designed so that AI-generated results are stored in structured formats wherever possible, allowing one workflow's output to become the input for another workflow. For example, the structured output of the Resume Agent can become an input to the Matching Agent, while the Matching Agent's skill-gap output can become an input to the Career Planning Agent and Interview Agent. This creates a connected chain rather than a collection of unrelated AI features.

The central product philosophy is that CareerPilot should feel like an AI career companion rather than an AI chatbot. The user should not have to repeatedly ask disconnected questions such as “What skills should I learn?”, “Does my resume match this job?”, “What interview questions should I prepare?”, and “What should I do next?” The platform should proactively connect these questions into one understandable journey: understand the user's current profile, understand the desired role, identify the gap, create a plan, help the user execute that plan, and then prepare the user to demonstrate those skills in an interview. The product therefore focuses on actionable intelligence rather than simply generating large amounts of AI text. Every AI output should ideally answer one of three things: what the user has, what the user is missing, and what the user should do next.

The long-term vision is for CareerPilot to become a continuously evolving personal career workspace. A user could begin with a basic resume, select a target role, receive a gap analysis, follow a personalized roadmap, complete projects, update their skills, practice interviews, and track applications without leaving the platform. As the user's profile changes, the system can regenerate relevant recommendations and adjust the preparation journey. Future versions could expand into job discovery, job-specific resume optimization, cover-letter assistance, GitHub/project analysis, LinkedIn profile analysis, application assistance, advanced mock interviews, and progress analytics. However, the initial product will deliberately focus on the core workflow of Resume → Target Job → Analysis → Skill Gap → Personalized Roadmap → Interview Preparation, ensuring that the first version solves a clear problem deeply rather than becoming a collection of unrelated AI features.

In essence, CareerPilot is designed to transform career preparation from a fragmented and confusing process into a structured, personalized journey. Instead of simply telling users what they should know, the product first understands who they are, understands where they want to go, measures the gap between the two, and then provides an actionable path to move forward. Lemma SDK provides the intelligent agent layer that makes this workflow adaptive and personalized, while the full-stack application provides the persistent user experience, data management, progress tracking, and interfaces required to turn those AI capabilities into a practical product.

End-to-End Product Flow — CareerPilot

1. Product Entry and Landing Experience

The complete journey begins when a user visits the CareerPilot website. The landing page should immediately communicate the core value proposition: the platform helps users understand their current career readiness, compare themselves against a target job, identify missing skills, create a personalized preparation roadmap, and practice interviews with an AI career coach. Instead of presenting the product as a generic AI assistant, the landing page should visually communicate the complete journey from Resume → Target Job → Skill Gap → Career Plan → Interview Preparation. The user should have clear actions such as Get Started, Analyze My Resume, or Build My Career Plan. The landing page can also show a simplified example of the product's output, such as a sample resume analysis, skill-gap card, or career roadmap, so the user immediately understands what they will receive after signing up.

The first interaction should be intentionally simple. The user should not be overwhelmed with a large form or multiple configuration options. The primary CTA takes the user into authentication and onboarding, after which the platform progressively collects the information needed to personalize the experience.



2. Authentication Flow

When the user clicks Get Started, they enter the authentication flow.

The user can either create an account using email/password or use Google authentication. After successful authentication, the backend creates or retrieves the user's account and establishes an authenticated session. The frontend then checks whether the user is a new user or an existing user.

For a new user:

Landing Page

      ↓

Sign Up

      ↓

Authentication

      ↓

Create User

      ↓

Onboarding

For an existing user:

Landing Page

      ↓

Login

      ↓

Authentication

      ↓

Retrieve Profile

      ↓

Dashboard

The backend should ensure that every user's career information is isolated from other users. Authentication and authorization middleware should protect private APIs so that a user can only access their own resumes, job descriptions, career plans, interviews, and applications.



3. First-Time Onboarding

After the first successful login, the user enters the onboarding experience. The purpose of onboarding is to establish the minimum amount of career context required to make the AI useful.

This information is stored in MongoDB and becomes the initial context for the AI workflows.

29. Final End-to-End Experience

At the end of the complete journey, the user should feel that CareerPilot has accompanied them throughout the entire preparation process. They start with an existing resume and an uncertain career goal. CareerPilot understands their current profile, analyzes a real target job, explains the differences between their current capabilities and the job's requirements, creates a personalized roadmap to close those gaps, helps them practice questions related to the role and their own projects, tracks their preparation, and allows them to connect that preparation to actual job applications. As the user learns new technologies, completes projects, improves their interview answers, and updates their resume, the platform can continuously reassess their profile and adjust recommendations. The end-to-end experience therefore moves beyond a single AI interaction and becomes a persistent cycle of Profile → Job → Gap → Plan → Practice → Progress → Reassessment, with Lemma-powered agents providing the intelligence at each major decision point.

Complete Technical Flow + Technology Stack

1. Overall Technical Architecture

CareerPilot will be designed as a full-stack web application with an AI agent layer powered by Lemma SDK. The architecture will follow a layered approach in which the frontend is responsible for the user interface and interactions, the backend acts as the central application and business-logic layer, MongoDB stores persistent user and career data, and Lemma-powered agents handle the intelligent analysis and decision-making workflows. The most important architectural principle is that Lemma should sit behind the backend rather than being directly exposed to the browser. This keeps API credentials secure, allows the backend to control what information is sent to the AI, enables validation of AI-generated outputs, and makes it possible to combine AI results with application data before returning a response to the user.

The overall architecture will be:

                         USER

                           │

                           │

                    HTTPS / REST API

                           │

                           ▼

                  Node.js + Express

                           │

          │                │                │

          ▼                ▼                ▼

      MongoDB          File Storage     Lemma SDK

          │                │                │

          │                │       ┌────────┼────────┐

          │                │       │        │        │

          │                │       ▼        ▼        ▼

          │                │    Resume     Job     Match

          │                │    Agent     Agent    Agent

          │                │       │        │        │

          │                │       └────────┼────────┘

          │                │                ▼

          │                │                │

          │                │                │

          │                │

The frontend can be implemented using React.js, with TypeScript recommended for better type safety and maintainability. Tailwind CSS can be used for the UI system, while React Router can handle navigation between dashboard, resume, job analysis, roadmap, interview, application, and profile pages. The backend will use Node.js with Express.js, exposing REST APIs to the frontend. MongoDB with Mongoose will provide the main persistent database. Resume files can be stored using a dedicated object-storage service, while MongoDB stores the file reference and extracted/analyzed information. The AI orchestration layer will use Lemma SDK, with individual workflows or agents responsible for resume analysis, job analysis, matching, career planning, and interview evaluation. Deployment can use Vercel for the frontend and a suitable Node.js hosting platform for the backend, with MongoDB Atlas providing managed database infrastructure.



2. Frontend Technical Architecture

The frontend will be the part of CareerPilot that users directly interact with. It will be responsible for rendering pages, collecting user input, displaying AI-generated results, maintaining temporary UI state, handling loading/error states, and communicating with the backend through secure HTTPS API requests. React.js + TypeScript should be used as the primary frontend stack because the application contains multiple interactive modules and shared components. Tailwind CSS will provide the styling system, while a component library can optionally be introduced if required for faster development. The frontend should be structured around reusable components rather than creating every screen independently.

A possible structure is:

client/

│

├── src/

│   ├── components/

│   ├── pages/

│   │   ├── Landing

│   │   ├── Login

│   ├── hooks/

│   ├── contexts/

│   ├── types/

│   ├── utils/

│   └── App.tsx

The frontend will communicate with the backend through REST APIs such as /api/auth, /api/resumes, /api/jobs, /api/matches, /api/career-plan, /api/interviews, and /api/applications. Axios or the native Fetch API can be used for HTTP communication. The frontend should maintain a clear separation between API communication and UI components. For example, the Dashboard component should not contain the actual HTTP request implementation; instead, a service such as dashboardService can communicate with the backend and return structured data to the UI.



3. Authentication Flow

Authentication will begin from the frontend when a user chooses to create an account or log in. The recommended options are Google OAuth and email/password authentication. When the user logs in, the frontend sends the authentication request to the backend. The backend validates the credentials or OAuth response, retrieves or creates the corresponding MongoDB user record, and establishes an authenticated session.

A secure flow should look like:

React

  ↓

Login Request

  ↓

Express Auth Route

  ↓

Authentication Service

  ↓

Validate User

  ↓

Create Session / Token

  ↓

React

  ↓

Authenticated Dashboard

If JWT-based authentication is used, tokens should be handled securely, preferably through HTTP-only cookies rather than exposing long-lived tokens to JavaScript unnecessarily. Protected Express middleware will verify authentication before allowing access to private resources. Every protected request should establish the user's identity before accessing resumes, jobs, interviews, career plans, or applications.



4. User Profile Data Flow

After authentication, the user profile is stored in MongoDB. The profile contains high-level information such as name, experience level, target role, career interests, and other preferences. This information becomes part of the context supplied to relevant Lemma workflows.

├── email

├── careerInterests

├── skills

├── createdAt

└── updatedAt

When the frontend requests the dashboard, the backend retrieves the user's profile and related career information from MongoDB and returns a structured response. The frontend then converts that response into dashboard cards, progress indicators, skill sections, and recommendations.



5. Resume Upload Technical Flow

Resume processing is one of the first major backend workflows. The user selects a PDF from the React interface. The frontend sends the file using multipart/form-data to an Express endpoint such as:

POST /api/resumes

The backend uses a file-upload middleware to receive and validate the document. It checks file type and size before accepting it. The actual file should be stored in object storage rather than inside MongoDB as a large binary document. MongoDB stores metadata such as the file URL/reference, upload timestamp, user ID, processing status, extracted text, and analysis result.

The technical flow becomes:

React

 ↓

PDF Upload

 ↓

Express

 ↓

File Validation

 ↓

Object Storage

 ↓

File Reference → MongoDB

 ↓

Text Extraction

 ↓

Resume Processing

A resume-processing service then extracts text from the uploaded PDF. The extracted text becomes the raw input for the AI analysis workflow.



6. Resume Analysis Using Lemma

Once the text has been extracted, the backend passes the relevant information to the Resume Analysis Agent through Lemma SDK. The backend should not simply send random application data to the agent. Instead, it should construct a controlled context containing the resume text and, where useful, the user's declared target role.

The flow becomes:

PDF

 ↓

Extracted Text

 ↓

Resume Service

 ↓

 ↓

Lemma Resume Agent

 ↓

Structured Resume Analysis

 ↓

Validate Output

 ↓

MongoDB

 ↓

React

The Resume Agent should return structured information such as skills, technologies, projects, experience, education, achievements, and potentially inferred career domains. The backend should validate the returned structure before storing it. This is important because downstream agents will depend on this information. If the AI returns malformed or incomplete data, the backend should handle the error rather than allowing broken data to propagate through the system.

24. Error Handling

AI applications need strong error handling because external AI calls, file processing, and network requests can fail.

For example:

Resume Upload

      ↓

Extraction Failed

      ↓

Return Processing Error

      ↓

Allow Retry

If Lemma does not return a valid response:

Lemma Request

      ↓

Invalid / Failed Response

      ↓

Backend Validation

      ↓

Log Error

      ↓

Retry if appropriate

      ↓

Fallback Error Response

The frontend should never expose internal errors, API keys, stack traces, or provider-specific credentials.

Instead, the user should see something understandable:

"We couldn't analyze your resume right now. Please try again."



25. Security Architecture

Because CareerPilot handles resumes and personal career information, security needs to be part of the architecture from the beginning.

The backend should implement:

Authentication 

Authorization 

Password hashing 

Secure sessions/tokens 

HTTPS 

Input validation 

File validation 

File-size limits 

Rate limiting 

CORS configuration 

Secure HTTP headers 

Environment variables for secrets 

User-level data isolation 

Protection against prompt injection 

Logging without exposing sensitive information 

AI-generated content should also be treated as untrusted output. The backend should validate structured AI responses before storing or using them.



26. Prompt Injection Protection

This is particularly important because the system processes external text such as resumes and job descriptions.

A malicious job description could theoretically contain instructions such as:

"Ignore your previous instructions..."

The system should treat job descriptions and resumes as data, not as instructions to the AI system.

The conceptual architecture should therefore distinguish:

SYSTEM / AGENT INSTRUCTIONS

             +

APPLICATION CONTEXT

             +

UNTRUSTED USER CONTENT

The untrusted content should never be allowed to override the agent's actual task.



27. Background Processing

Some operations may take longer than normal API requests, especially resume processing and complex AI workflows.

Instead of making the user wait indefinitely:

Upload

 ↓

 ↓

 ↓

Lemma Analysis

 ↓

 ↓

28. Caching and Performance

Frequently accessed information such as the dashboard, career profile, and job analysis can be cached where appropriate. However, AI-generated results should generally be persisted in MongoDB rather than regenerated every time the user opens a page.

For example, after analyzing a resume:

First request:

Resume → Lemma → Analysis → MongoDB



Future requests:

Frontend → Backend → MongoDB

The AI should only be called again when the user explicitly requests re-analysis or when the underlying data has changed enough to justify a new analysis.

33. Final Technical Concept

The most important technical concept behind CareerPilot is that the application is not simply sending user messages to an AI model and displaying the response. It is a structured full-stack system in which user information is collected, normalized, stored, analyzed, transformed into structured career intelligence, and then reused across multiple specialized AI workflows. React provides the interactive experience, Node.js and Express provide the secure application and business-logic layer, MongoDB provides persistent career memory, object storage manages uploaded resume files, and Lemma SDK provides the intelligent agent layer. The output of each major AI workflow becomes structured input for the next stage: the Resume Agent produces the career profile, the Job Agent produces the job requirement profile, the Matching Agent produces the comparison, the Skill Gap workflow produces actionable gaps, the Career Planner produces the roadmap, and the Interview Agent uses all of that context to create personalized interview preparation. This creates a continuous technical loop rather than isolated AI features: User Data → Resume Intelligence → Job Intelligence → Matching → Skill Gap → Personalized Plan → Practice → Progress → Re-analysis.

The entire CareerPilot experience should be built around one visual idea: “Your career journey, mapped clearly from where you are to where you want to go.” The interface should feel like a combination of a modern productivity application, a premium career platform, and a personal coaching workspace. InterviewQuestion

FeedbackBlock

ApplicationCard

This will make the entire product visually consistent.



40. Dashboard Information Hierarchy

The dashboard should always follow this order:

1. WHERE AM I?

   Career readiness



2. WHERE AM I GOING?

   Target role



3. WHAT SHOULD I DO NOW?

   Next action



4. WHAT AM I MISSING?

   Skill gaps



5. HOW AM I IMPROVING?

   Career plan



6. AM I READY?

   Interview performance

This is much better than throwing every metric onto the first screen.



41. Microcopy

The copy should be human and direct.

Avoid:

“Our sophisticated AI engine has identified potential optimization opportunities.”

Use:

You're missing Docker for this role. Here's what to do next.

Avoid:

“Generate personalized learning trajectory.”

Use:

Build my preparation plan

Avoid:

“Initiate intelligent interview simulation.”

Use:

Start interview

This will make the product feel less AI-generated and more like a real product.



42. The Standout Feature: “Next Move”

I would make Next Move a signature element throughout the application.

Every important screen can answer:

What should I do next?

For example:

Dashboard

Complete Docker preparation

Resume

Add missing project evidence

Job Analysis

Review your 2 missing skills

Career Plan

Continue AWS deployment

Interview

Practice your weakest topic

Application

Prepare for your interview

This gives the entire product a consistent personality.



43. The Signature Career Journey Visualization

The product should have one recurring visual element across the dashboard.

YOU ARE HERE



● Profile

│

● Resume

│

● Job Match

│

● Skill Gaps

│

● Career Plan

│

○ Interview

│

○ Application

Completed stages are visually muted/solid, the current stage is highlighted with the orange accent, and future stages remain subtle.

This can appear on the dashboard as a compact horizontal journey:

PROFILE ─── RESUME ─── MATCH ─── GAP ─── PLAN ─── INTERVIEW

                         ↑

                       YOU ARE HERE

That becomes the visual identity of CareerPilot.



44. Complete Screen Map

The final product should contain approximately these screens:

PUBLIC

45. Complete Visual Journey

The user should experience the product like this:

                         CAREERPILOT



                              ↓



                    "Where do you want to go?"



                              ↓

                      "Let's understand you."

                      AI CAREER PROFILE



                              ↓



                 "Now show me the job."



                              ↓



                       ADD JOB DESCRIPTION



                              ↓



                      JOB INTELLIGENCE



                              ↓



                    ┌───────────────────┐

                    │ YOUR PROFILE      │

                    │        ↕          │

                    │ TARGET JOB        │

                    └───────────────────┘



                              ↓



                        SKILL GAP



                              ↓



                  "Here's what you're missing."



                              ↓



                      CAREER ROADMAP



                              ↓



                    "Here's what to do."



                              ↓



                     USER TAKES ACTION



                              ↓



                      INTERVIEW COACH



                              ↓



                    "Let's test your skills."



                              ↓



                       FEEDBACK



                              ↓



                      IMPROVEMENT



                              ↓



                    JOB APPLICATION



                              ↓



                 "You're preparing for THIS job."



                              ↓



                       RE-ANALYSIS



                              ↓



                    UPDATED CAREER PROFILE



46. Final UI/UX Philosophy

The most important thing is that CareerPilot should never feel like five separate AI tools placed inside one website. The Resume page, Job Analysis page, Skill Gap page, Career Plan, Interview Coach, and Application Tracker should all feel like different stages of the same career journey.

The visual language should remain consistent: white/off-white canvas, charcoal typography, restrained orange accent, thin borders, generous whitespace, subtle motion, strong hierarchy, and minimal decorative noise. The product should prioritize information clarity over flashy AI effects. Every screen should have one obvious primary action. Every AI result should lead to a practical next step. Every major user action should update the user's persistent career state.

The central UX loop should always remain visible:

Understand me → Understand the job → Show me the gap → Tell me what to do → Help me practice → Show my progress.

That is what should make the product stand out—not excessive animations or AI gimmicks, but the feeling that the entire application understands where the user is in their career journey and always knows what the next useful action is.

matchedSkills.name: Docker
matchedSkills.evidence: Declared as a core skill alongside the backend service work in the 'Full Stack Cloud Workspace' project, where the candidate engineered backend services with token auth and database caching — a container-friendly delivery context. Containerization is claimed as a working tool, not just exposure.

matchedSkills.name: Git
matchedSkills.evidence: Listed as a core skill and implicitly required by the '2023 - Present' Full Stack Developer role building microservices with high test coverage, which depends on branch/merge-based collaboration.

matchedSkills.name: JavaScript / TypeScript
matchedSkills.evidence: Primary language pair across both projects: the Full Stack Cloud Workspace lists JavaScript and TypeScript, and the Real-Time Collaborative Dashboard was built in a JS/React/Node stack.

matchedSkills.name: Node.js / Express
matchedSkills.evidence: Used to build the backend of the Real-Time Collaborative Dashboard (WebSocket-enabled, sub-100ms sync with state persistence) and the services layer of the Full Stack Cloud Workspace, plus REST APIs, PostgreSQL and Redis caching.

partialSkills.name: CI/CD
partialSkills.currentLevel: Git-based version control and manual/ad-hoc build-test runs (has 'high test coverage' but no pipeline evidence)
partialSkills.requiredLevel: Production CI/CD pipeline ownership: automated build, test, container-image publish, and gated deployment across environments
partialSkills.gapExplanation: The candidate has the raw materials a pipeline is built from — Git, Docker, a tested codebase — but the profile shows no CI/CD platform (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI, CircleCI) and no evidence of automating build/test/deploy or managing environment promotion and rollback. Writing tests that run locally is materially different from owning a pipeline that blocks merges and ships on a schedule.
partialSkills.recommendation: Add a GitHub Actions workflow to one existing project that on push runs the test suite, builds and pushes a Docker image to a registry, and deploys it to a staging environment with a manual approval gate; document the YAML in the repo so the pipeline itself is the artifact of proof.

partialSkills.name: System Design
partialSkills.currentLevel: Service-level design: microservices and database caching (Redis) implemented inside a single product
partialSkills.requiredLevel: Distributed, multi-region system design: topology, failure domains, data replication, failover, and capacity/cost trade-offs
partialSkills.gapExplanation: The candidate's microservice and caching work is real but scoped to one region and one product, with no stated requirements on availability, latency budgets, or blast radius. Datadog's role wants design that reasons about regions, replication and resilience, which is a different order of abstraction than wiring services together.
partialSkills.recommendation: Do a written design exercise: produce a one-page architecture doc for a multi-region deployment of the Real-Time Collaborative Dashboard (region layout, data replication strategy, failover, and why), then have it reviewed or publish it as a repo README.

missingSkills.name: Kubernetes
missingSkills.impactOnRole: This is the single biggest screening gate. The job's first responsibility is managing multi-region Kubernetes clusters, so an interview will move quickly to pods, deployments, services, ingress, autoscaling, and failure recovery. Without it the candidate cannot discuss the day-to-day work of the role at all, and a resume screen against a Datadog DevOps req is likely to filter out before a human reads it.
missingSkills.recommendation: Deploy the containerized Full Stack Cloud Workspace to a managed Kubernetes cluster (k3s locally first, then a cloud-managed control plane): write Deployment, Service, Ingress and ConfigMap manifests, set resource requests/limits and a horizontal pod autoscaler, then deliberately kill a pod and document the recovery. Commit the manifests and a short runbook.

missingSkills.name: AWS
missingSkills.impactOnRole: Required skill with no cloud provider anywhere in the profile — Docker and Redis are used, but nothing indicates where they run. Datadog's platform work assumes fluency with core AWS building blocks (IAM, VPC/networking, EKS, S3, RDS, CloudWatch) and especially IAM and networking boundaries, since misconfigured permissions are the most common failure mode in a managed cluster. This blocks both screening and any practical infrastructure conversation.
missingSkills.recommendation: Ship one AWS project end to end: run the app on EKS behind an Application Load Balancer, use IAM roles for service accounts instead of static keys, put secrets in Secrets Manager or SSM, and add CloudWatch logs/alarms — then write up the IAM and network boundary decisions in the repo.

missingSkills.name: Security Compliance
missingSkills.impactOnRole: The role's second stated responsibility pairs CI with security compliance, so container image scanning, secret management, least-privilege IAM, and dependency/SBOM hygiene are expected as part of the pipeline rather than a separate team's job. The profile shows token auth but no scanning or compliance controls, so the candidate would struggle on the 'ensure security compliance' half of the mandate.
missingSkills.recommendation: Add automated security gates to the CI pipeline: image vulnerability scanning (Trivy or Grype), dependency audit, and secret scanning, set them to fail the build on critical findings, and document the triage policy for a flagged CVE.

missingSkills.name: Python
missingSkills.impactOnRole: A preferred skill, and the lingua franca of cloud/DevOps tooling, automation scripts, and platform glue code. Being JS/TS-only narrows the candidate to Node-based tooling and is an easy differentiator against other DevOps candidates during a technical screen.
missingSkills.recommendation: Rewrite one operational script (e.g. a cluster/image cleanup or health-check script) in Python using the AWS SDK for Python (boto3) and the Kubernetes client library, and commit it with tests alongside the JavaScript version.

matches.nextMove: Containerize the Full Stack Cloud Workspace and deploy it to a managed Kubernetes cluster on AWS (EKS) with a GitHub Actions pipeline that builds the image, scans it, and deploys it — this one project simultaneously closes the Kubernetes, AWS, CI/CD and security-compliance gaps and gives you a single repo to talk through in the interview.

careerPlans.nextTask: Containerize Full-Stack App with Multi-Stage Dockerfile

phases.title: Phase 1: Core Fundamentals & Code Quality
phases.description: Establish a container-first development baseline for a Full Stack Engineer role. While the candidate owns baseline web development, every task here forces the containerization, testing, and CI discipline that the Docker and AWS gaps demand: you cannot ship to ECS or run distributed infrastructure if your local build, lint, test, and CI loop is not reproducible inside a container.

tasks.title: Containerize the Local Full-Stack Dev Environment
tasks.description: Take an existing Full Stack app (or a new reference app: React/Next.js frontend + Node/Express or FastAPI backend + Postgres) and define it entirely in containers. Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for the backend (deps -> build -> runtime) and one for the frontend, then a docker-compose.yml wiring frontend, backend, and Postgres with named volumes, a shared network, environment variables via .env, and a healthcheck on the DB. Add bind mounts for hot reload in dev and document the single-command startup.
tasks.deliverable: Optimized multi-stage Dockerfile for the backend and frontend plus a docker-compose.yml with hot reload, named volumes, and DB healthchecks; README section proving `docker compose up` boots the full stack from a clean machine.

tasks.title: Enforce Language-Level Code Quality Gates
tasks.description: Harden the baseline every Full Stack Engineer is expected to ship with. Enable TypeScript strict mode (or Python type checking with mypy/pyright), configure ESLint + Prettier (or Ruff + Black), and add a Husky/lint-staged pre-commit hook that blocks non-conforming commits. Define npm scripts so the exact same lint/typecheck commands can be invoked inside the Docker build and in CI.
tasks.deliverable: Committed ESLint/Prettier (or Ruff/Black) config, TypeScript strict tsconfig (or mypy config), and a Husky pre-commit hook; a documented `lint` and `typecheck` script that runs identically locally and in a container.

tasks.title: Container-Aware Automated Test Suite
tasks.description: Prove the app is testable in isolation, the way it will be tested in a pipeline. Add unit tests for business logic and integration tests for API routes that run against a real Postgres instance spun up with Testcontainers (or a dedicated compose service). Cover at least one happy path, one validation error, and one auth/permission case for the core resource.
tasks.deliverable: Vitest/Jest + Supertest (or Pytest) suite running integration tests against a Testcontainers Postgres, with a coverage report and a `test` script that executes against containers with no manually pre-started database.

tasks.title: CI Pipeline with Lint + Test Matrix
tasks.description: Wire the container-first workflow into continuous integration. Create a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on every PR: installs deps with caching, runs lint/typecheck, runs the test suite, and builds the Docker images (without pushing yet). Use a matrix across the supported Node/Python version and add branch protection requiring the checks to pass before merge.
tasks.deliverable: GitHub Actions workflow with lint and test matrix plus an image-build job; enabled branch protection requiring green checks, and a screenshot/link of a passing PR pipeline.

phases.title: Phase 2: High-Priority Missing Skill Deep Dive
phases.description: Close the Docker gap to a production bar. Phase 1 made the app runnable in containers; this phase makes those images small, secure, observable, and orchestrated as multiple independent services, which is exactly the container literacy an AWS/ECS-based Full Stack Engineer is hired for.

tasks.title: Production-Grade Image Optimization
tasks.description: Rebuild the images for production: use slim/alpine or distroless base images, run as a non-root user, copy only build artifacts into the runtime stage, add a proper .dockerignore, set OCI labels, and use multi-arch builds. Pin base image digests and layer the Dockerfile so dependency layers cache across code changes. Measure the before/after image size with `docker image ls` and `dive`.
tasks.deliverable: Hardened production Dockerfile producing a sub-300MB runtime image running as non-root with a pinned base digest, a committed .dockerignore, and a size/layer report comparing dev vs production images.

tasks.title: Multi-Service Orchestration with Compose
tasks.description: Model a realistic distributed stack locally: frontend, API, background worker, Postgres, Redis, and an Nginx reverse proxy. Define separate dev and prod compose files with overrides, custom networks isolating the DB from the public tier, healthcheck-based `depends_on`, resource limits, and JSON-file log rotation. Seed the DB and confirm data persists across restarts.
tasks.deliverable: docker-compose.yml + docker-compose.override/prod files orchestrating six services with isolated networks, healthchecks, resource limits, and log rotation; a verified `docker compose down && up` preserving volumes plus a service-topology diagram.

tasks.title: Container Security & Supply-Chain Scanning
tasks.description: Treat images as untrusted artifacts. Scan images with Trivy (or Grype) for CVEs, generate an SBOM with Syft, remove secrets from layers, and adopt a secrets strategy (build secrets / env injection rather than baked-in keys). Add the scanner as a CI job that fails on HIGH/CRITICAL findings and document the remediation of at least three real findings.
tasks.deliverable: CI-integrated Trivy scan job, generated SBOM file, a secrets-handling policy, and a remediation log showing three CVEs found and fixed.

tasks.title: Container Debugging & Runtime Performance Runbook
tasks.description: Learn to operate containers, not just build them. Use `docker logs`, `docker exec`, `docker stats`, `docker inspect`, and `docker events` to diagnose a deliberately broken service (crash loop, OOM, port conflict, network DNS failure). Apply memory/CPU limits and demonstrate graceful shutdown by handling SIGTERM in the app. Write a runbook covering the symptoms and fixes you actually reproduced.
tasks.deliverable: Container debugging runbook (5 reproduced incidents with root cause and fix), demonstrated SIGTERM graceful shutdown, and a `docker stats` before/after report under applied resource limits.

phases.title: Phase 3: Cloud Deployment & Distributed Infrastructure
phases.description: Close the AWS gap by taking the Dockerized application into a real cloud environment. This phase moves from a single laptop to managed AWS infrastructure provisioned as code, so the candidate can speak and work credibly about ECS, ECR, RDS, and CI/CD in a Full Stack Engineer interview.

tasks.title: AWS Account Baseline with Least-Privilege IAM as Code
tasks.description: Set up a clean AWS foundation: a dedicated (non-root) admin identity with MFA, a least-privilege IAM user/role for deployment, the AWS CLI v2 configured with profiles, and a billing alarm/budget. Provision all of it as Terraform (or AWS CDK) in a version-controlled repo with a remote state backend in S3 + DynamoDB locking, rather than clicking in the console.
tasks.deliverable: Terraform repo provisioning IAM roles/policies, budget alarms, and an S3+DynamoDB remote-state backend; least-privilege deployment policy documented and a screenshot of the active budget alarm.

tasks.title: Deploy Containers to ECS Fargate behind an ALB
tasks.description: Take the Phase 2 production images to the cloud. Push them to Amazon ECR, define ECS task definitions and a Fargate service across two Availability Zones, and front it with an Application Load Balancer plus target-group health checks. Place tasks in private subnets and expose only the ALB via a security group. Provision the whole stack in Terraform with variable-driven environments.
tasks.deliverable: Terraform-provisioned ECR repository, ECS Fargate service (2+ AZs, private subnets), and ALB with health checks; a reachable public URL serving the app plus a deployed-architecture diagram.

tasks.title: Managed Data & Secrets on AWS
tasks.description: Replace local containers with managed services. Provision RDS Postgres in private subnets with a security group accepting traffic only from the ECS service, a versioned S3 bucket with a least-privilege bucket policy for uploads, and AWS Secrets Manager (or SSM Parameter Store) for DB credentials and app secrets injected at task start. Migrate schema and confirm the app reads/writes managed data.
tasks.deliverable: Terraform-provisioned RDS Postgres + S3 bucket + Secrets Manager entries, security-group wiring restricting DB access to ECS, a migration run against RDS, and proof of a file upload persisted to S3.

tasks.title: GitHub Actions CI/CD to AWS with OIDC and Rollback
tasks.description: Automate delivery without static AWS keys. Configure GitHub OIDC federation to an IAM role, then extend the CI pipeline to build the image, push to ECR, render the new task definition, and perform a rolling ECS deployment that waits for stability. Add a manual approval gate for production and a documented rollback (re-deploy the previous task revision).
tasks.deliverable: OIDC-based GitHub Actions deploy workflow (build -> ECR -> ECS rolling deploy), IAM trust policy, and a tested rollback procedure with logs showing a successful deploy and a successful rollback.

phases.title: Phase 4: Production Architecture & Scalability
phases.description: Move from 'it deploys' to 'it survives'. This phase builds the operational and architectural depth (observability, autoscaling, caching, async processing, cost and multi-environment control) that separates a mid-level Full Stack Engineer from a senior one, using the AWS and Docker skills established earlier.

tasks.title: Observability: Logging, Metrics, and Alarms
tasks.description: Instrument the deployed stack. Emit structured JSON logs from the app, ship them to CloudWatch Logs, and publish custom business + latency metrics via the CloudWatch SDK (or embedded metric format). Create a dashboard (request rate, p95 latency, error rate, ECS CPU/memory) and alarms that fire on error-rate and latency thresholds, plus a request-ID correlation approach across ALB -> app -> worker.
tasks.deliverable: Structured-logging middleware, a CloudWatch dashboard, at least three CloudWatch alarms (error rate, p95 latency, unhealthy targets), and a documented trace of one request across services via correlation IDs.

tasks.title: Autoscaling & Load Testing Under Real Traffic
tasks.description: Make the service elastic and prove it. Configure ECS Service Auto Scaling using target-tracking on CPU and ALB request-count-per-target, then generate load with k6 (or Locust) against the deployed endpoint. Capture p95 latency, throughput, and error rate before and after scaling kicks in, and tune the target value, cooldowns, and min/max task counts to hit a defined SLO.
tasks.deliverable: ECS autoscaling policies (CPU + ALB request count) with tuned min/max, a k6/Locust load-test script, and a load-test report (throughput, p95, errors) showing scale-out behaviour under load.

tasks.title: Caching and Asynchronous Processing at Scale
tasks.description: Remove synchronous bottlenecks. Introduce ElastiCache (Redis) with a cache-aside pattern for a hot read endpoint, and move slow work (email, image processing, report generation) to a background worker consuming an SQS queue with a dead-letter queue and idempotent processing. Containerize the worker with its own image and run it as a separate ECS service.
tasks.deliverable: Redis cache-aside layer with measured hit-rate/latency improvement, an SQS-backed worker as a separate ECS service with a DLQ, and a before/after latency benchmark for the cached endpoint.

tasks.title: Multi-Environment, Cost, and Disaster-Recovery Discipline
tasks.description: Make the infrastructure repeatable and affordable. Parameterize Terraform into dev/staging/prod workspaces (or var-files) with environment-specific sizing, stand up a second environment end-to-end, produce an AWS Cost Explorer analysis with three concrete optimizations (rightsizing Fargate, RDS instance class, savings from caching), and document an RTO/RPO backup-and-restore runbook for RDS and S3.
tasks.deliverable: Multi-environment Terraform (dev/staging/prod) with a deployed staging stack, a cost analysis with three applied optimizations, and a tested backup/restore DR runbook with measured recovery time.

phases.title: Phase 5: Technical Interview Polish & Review
phases.description: Convert the hands-on work into interview performance. Every deliverable built in Phases 1-4 becomes a story, a diagram, and a defensible design decision. This phase rehearses system design, consolidates AWS knowledge, hardens the portfolio, and drills behavioral answers for the Full Stack Engineer loop.

tasks.title: System Design Drills Anchored in the Built Stack
tasks.description: Practice designing systems out loud using your own architecture as the reference. Produce written design docs for three prompts (a URL shortener, a multi-tenant SaaS API, and an image-upload/processing pipeline) covering API contracts, data model, caching, queueing, container/hosting topology on AWS, scaling, and failure modes. Whiteboard each with boxes-and-arrows diagrams and time yourself to 35 minutes.
tasks.deliverable: Three written system design documents with architecture diagrams, tradeoff tables, and a self-review noting where an interviewer would push back.

tasks.title: Harden and Document the Portfolio Repository
tasks.description: Turn the project into evidence. Consolidate the code, Terraform, compose files, CI workflows, tests, and runbooks into one clean public repository with a compelling README: problem statement, architecture diagram, tech stack, local `docker compose up` quickstart, AWS deployment guide, screenshots, cost notes, and the CVE remediation/load-test results from earlier phases.
tasks.deliverable: Public GitHub repository with an architecture diagram, Docker quickstart, AWS deployment guide, screenshots, and a RESUME.md mapping each project feature to a resume bullet.

tasks.title: AWS Knowledge Consolidation and Practice Exams
tasks.description: Convert practical AWS experience into exam-grade, interview-ready fluency. Work through the core SAA-C03 (or Cloud Practitioner as a checkpoint) domains: IAM, VPC/networking, ECS/ECR/Fargate, RDS, S3, SQS, CloudWatch, and cost models. Summarize each service into a one-page cheat sheet and sit at least three timed practice exams, reviewing every wrong answer to a service-level explanation.
tasks.deliverable: AWS service cheat-sheets (10+ services) and three timed practice-exam score reports with a wrong-answer review log; a target of consistent 80%+ before scheduling the real exam.

tasks.title: Mock Interviews and STAR Story Bank
tasks.description: Rehearse the full Full Stack Engineer loop: a live coding round (containers + a tested API endpoint), a Docker/AWS deep-dive, and behavioral questions. Build a STAR story bank from your real Phase 1-4 work (e.g. 'cut image size 1.2GB -> 200MB', 'diagnosed an ECS OOM crash loop', 'designed the multi-service compose stack'), run two mock interviews with a peer or recorded video, and log every question with a tightened answer.
tasks.deliverable: STAR story bank with 8+ stories tied to concrete metrics, two recorded mock-interview sessions, and a question log with revised answers plus a final readiness checklist.

careerPlans.summary: A 10-week, container-and-cloud-first roadmap for a Full Stack Engineer candidate whose two priority gaps are Docker and AWS. It is sequenced so each phase feeds the next: build a reproducible containerized dev/test/CI loop, harden images and multi-service orchestration, deploy that stack as code onto AWS (ECR, ECS Fargate, RDS, S3, Secrets Manager), then add production depth (CloudWatch observability, autoscaling under real load, Redis + SQS async processing, multi-environment Terraform and cost control), and finally convert every artifact into interview-ready system-design docs, a documented portfolio repo, AWS exam fluency, and STAR stories. Every task names the specific gap it closes and produces a concrete, inspectable deliverable.

phases.title: Phase 1: Core Fundamentals & Code Quality
phases.description: Establish the engineering baseline a Stripe full-stack role assumes: a reproducible containerized local environment and automated code-quality gates. Your Azure/network operations background is strong, but you must now prove you can build and ship application code with the same rigor you apply to firewall policy. This phase converts your ops discipline into developer workflow discipline.

tasks.title: Containerize a local full-stack dev environment
tasks.description: Take a Node.js REST API + Postgres app and make it fully reproducible on any machine. Write a Dockerfile for the API and a docker-compose.yml that runs API, Postgres, and Redis together with named volumes, a shared bridge network, and bind-mounted source for hot reload. Reproduce the exact local setup from a clean clone in a single `docker compose up`.
tasks.deliverable: Dockerfile + docker-compose.yml that boots API, Postgres, and Redis with one command, plus a README with reset/teardown steps

tasks.title: Build a lint, typecheck, and test CI pipeline
tasks.description: Create a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on every pull request: install with a cached dependency step, run ESLint, TypeScript typecheck, and the Jest/Vitest suite against a Postgres service container. Add a build matrix across two Node versions and fail the job on lint or test errors. Frame each job the way you would frame a change-management gate: nothing merges without evidence.
tasks.deliverable: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with lint, typecheck, and a test matrix running against a Postgres service container

tasks.title: Produce a hardened multi-stage production image
tasks.description: Refactor the dev Dockerfile into a multi-stage build: builder stage compiles TypeScript and installs dev dependencies, runtime stage copies only production artifacts, runs as a non-root user, and includes a HEALTHCHECK. Add a .dockerignore. Scan the image with Trivy and remediate critical CVEs. This mirrors the least-privilege posture you already enforce in firewall audits.
tasks.deliverable: Optimized multi-stage Dockerfile with non-root runtime and HEALTHCHECK, a .dockerignore, and a Trivy scan report showing zero critical findings

tasks.title: Enforce quality gates with pre-commit hooks and branch protection
tasks.description: Add pre-commit hooks for formatting, linting, and secret detection, then configure branch protection so CI must pass before merge. Document the workflow as a short runbook, deliberately mapping it to the Change Advisory Board process you already run for firewall rule changes.
tasks.deliverable: `.pre-commit-config.yaml` plus a branch-protection runbook comparing the pipeline gates to your existing CAB change flow

phases.title: Phase 2: High-Priority Missing Skill Deep Dive
phases.description: Go deep on the three gaps that most block a full-stack hire: Docker in production, CI/CD beyond the basics, and Redis as a real application component. Every exercise is built around patterns a payments platform actually uses — idempotency, rate limiting, and safe release promotion — so the work doubles as interview material.

tasks.title: Implement a Redis-backed idempotency key service
tasks.description: Build a service that stores idempotency keys in Redis with TTLs, stores the response body alongside the key, and replays the stored response when a duplicate request arrives. Handle the concurrent-duplicate race with a Redis lock (SET NX with expiry) and cover the race with an integration test that fires parallel identical requests. This is the exact mechanic behind safe payment retries.
tasks.deliverable: Redis-backed idempotency middleware with TTL handling, a concurrency-safe Redis lock, and integration tests proving no duplicate side effects

tasks.title: Build a token-bucket rate limiter with Lua scripts
tasks.description: Implement a distributed rate limiter using Redis atomic Lua scripts so multiple app instances share one counter. Support per-API-key and per-IP limits, return proper 429 responses with Retry-After, and load-test it to confirm the limit holds under concurrency. Note in your README why rate limiting is a first-class concern for a payments API.
tasks.deliverable: Lua-backed token-bucket rate limiter module with configurable limits, 429 handling, and a load-test result confirming the limit is not exceeded

tasks.title: Design a production-grade Docker image and runtime policy
tasks.description: Push the Phase 1 image further: pin base image digests, add read-only root filesystem, drop Linux capabilities, set resource limits in compose, and configure graceful shutdown with a SIGTERM handler. Compare image layers before and after with `docker history` and document the size reduction in a short write-up.
tasks.deliverable: Hardened runtime configuration (digests pinned, read-only FS, dropped capabilities, resource limits, graceful shutdown) plus a before/after layer-size write-up

tasks.title: Build a multi-environment release pipeline with rollback
tasks.description: Extend CI into CD: on merge to main, publish a versioned Docker image to a registry, deploy to a staging environment, run smoke tests, then require a manual approval gate before promoting the same digest to production. Implement semantic version tagging and a documented one-step rollback. Treat the approval gate as a deliberate control, the way you treat firewall change approval today.
tasks.deliverable: Release workflow that builds a tagged image, deploys to staging, runs smoke tests, gates on manual approval, promotes the same digest to prod, and supports rollback — with a release runbook

tasks.title: Add real-time delivery with Redis Pub/Sub
tasks.description: Wire Redis Pub/Sub (or Streams) into the app so a payment-status update publishes an event and a WebSocket gateway pushes it to the browser. Add reconnect and backpressure handling. This demonstrates a full-stack real-time path and prepares you for event-driven design in Phase 4.
tasks.deliverable: Redis Pub/Sub or Streams integration with a WebSocket gateway, reconnect handling, and a short architecture note

phases.title: Phase 3: Cloud Deployment & Distributed Infrastructure
phases.description: Translate your Azure networking expertise into AWS. Your VNet, NSG, UDR, and firewalling knowledge maps directly onto VPC, security groups, route tables, and NACLs — so this phase lets you move fast while learning the AWS surface area. By the end your containerized app runs on AWS with managed Redis and a keyless CI/CD path.

tasks.title: Build an AWS VPC as a Terraform module, mapping from Azure
tasks.description: Provision a VPC with public and private subnets across two AZs, internet and NAT gateways, route tables, and layered security groups, all in Terraform. Explicitly document the concept mapping: Azure VNet to VPC, NSG to Security Group, UDR to route table, Azure Firewall egress rules to NACLs plus NAT. Migrate your existing mental model rather than starting cold.
tasks.deliverable: Reusable Terraform VPC module with public/private subnets and security groups, plus a side-by-side Azure-to-AWS networking concept mapping document

tasks.title: Deploy the containerized app to ECS Fargate behind an ALB
tasks.description: Push your image to ECR and run it on ECS Fargate in private subnets, fronted by an Application Load Balancer with a target group health check. Add a task definition with secrets pulled from AWS Secrets Manager and an auto-scaling policy on CPU and request count. Deliver a publicly reachable staging URL.
tasks.deliverable: Terraform-provisioned ECS Fargate service behind an ALB with health checks, Secrets Manager integration, auto-scaling, and a live staging URL

tasks.title: Attach managed Redis in a private subnet
tasks.description: Provision ElastiCache Redis with a subnet group and security group that only accepts traffic from the app's security group — the same least-privilege instinct you apply to NSG rules. Point the app's idempotency and rate-limiter code at it, enable at-rest and in-transit encryption, and verify the app works with no public Redis exposure.
tasks.deliverable: ElastiCache Redis reachable only from the app security group, with encryption enabled and the app confirmed working against managed Redis

tasks.title: Wire keyless CI/CD deployment to AWS with OIDC
tasks.description: Replace static AWS credentials with a GitHub OIDC trust relationship, then extend your pipeline to deploy the new task definition on merge. Add a blue/green or rolling deployment with automatic rollback on failed health checks. Document the trust policy and the principle of no long-lived cloud keys, echoing your policy-enforcement approach to credentials.
tasks.deliverable: GitHub OIDC IAM role, CI/CD deployment step to ECS, blue/green deployment with automatic rollback, and a trust-policy document

tasks.title: Port your Azure observability stack to CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry
tasks.description: Instrument the app with OpenTelemetry for traces, metrics, and structured logs shipping to CloudWatch. Build a dashboard for request rate, error rate, p95 latency, and Redis hit rate, and create alarms that page on sustained error rate. Deliberately map each element to the Azure Monitor and Log Analytics views you already operate.
tasks.deliverable: OpenTelemetry instrumentation plus a CloudWatch dashboard and alarm set, with a mapping table from Azure Monitor/Log Analytics to the AWS equivalents

phases.title: Phase 4: Production Architecture & Scalability
phases.description: Move from deployment to design. This phase builds the system-design muscle Stripe interviews test hardest: ledger and idempotency modeling, event-driven webhook delivery, caching and queue-backed scaling, and a security threat model that leverages your Palo Alto and segmentation experience. Every artifact is reusable as an interview answer.

tasks.title: Design a payment ledger and idempotency system
tasks.description: Write a full design doc for a payments service: double-entry ledger schema, idempotent charge API with request keys, state machine for payment lifecycle, transaction boundaries, and failure modes with recovery. Include an ER diagram, API contracts, and an explicit discussion of exactly-once vs at-least-once semantics. This is the single most likely Stripe design prompt.
tasks.deliverable: Design document with ER diagram, API contracts, payment state machine, and a failure-mode and recovery section

tasks.title: Build event-driven webhook delivery with retries and a dead-letter queue
tasks.description: Implement webhook delivery using a queue with exponential backoff, HMAC request signing, de-duplication, and a dead-letter queue for poison messages. Include a replay endpoint for failed deliveries and a test that simulates an endpoint returning 500s. Document the delivery guarantees.
tasks.deliverable: Queue-backed webhook delivery system with HMAC signing, exponential backoff, DLQ, replay endpoint, and a delivery-guarantees write-up

tasks.title: Prove scalability with caching plus load testing
tasks.description: Add a Redis cache-aside layer with explicit key design, TTL policy, and cache invalidation on write, then measure the effect. Load-test with k6 from a low to a spiking request profile, capture p50/p95/p99 latency and error rate before and after caching, and identify the first bottleneck. Document where Redis must not be used to avoid stale financial data.
tasks.deliverable: Cache-aside implementation with a documented TTL and invalidation strategy, plus a k6 load-test report showing p95/p99 latency before and after caching

tasks.title: Write a threat model and harden the stack's segmentation
tasks.description: Produce a STRIDE-based threat model of your deployed app, then close the highest risks in IaC: tighten security-group and NACL rules to least privilege, add WAF rules in front of the ALB, move all secrets out of source, and document data flows. Bring your Palo Alto rule-audit method to bear on removing permissive paths.
tasks.deliverable: STRIDE threat model document plus hardened Terraform showing least-privilege security groups, WAF rules, and a secrets inventory

phases.title: Phase 5: Technical Interview Polish & Review
phases.description: Convert the build work into interview performance. Drill system design and coding under time pressure, ship a portfolio capstone that demonstrates Docker, CI/CD, AWS, and Redis end to end, and reposition your resume from security operations toward full-stack engineering.

tasks.title: Run timed system design mock interviews
tasks.description: Complete six 45-minute mock designs, prioritizing payments-adjacent prompts: payment processing, idempotent APIs, a webhook platform, a rate-limited public API, a notification system, and a reconciliation pipeline. Peers or a mock-interview service should give feedback; record yourself and self-score against a rubric for requirements, estimation, API design, data model, scaling, and trade-offs.
tasks.deliverable: Six recorded mock sessions, each with a completed rubric self-score and a list of specific fixes for the next round

tasks.title: Drill full-stack coding under interview constraints
tasks.description: Solve 40 problems spanning data structures and algorithms plus practical full-stack exercises such as designing a REST endpoint with pagination, implementing a cache, and writing SQL for a many-to-many query. Practice out loud with a 30-minute timer so explanation quality, not just correctness, is trained.
tasks.deliverable: A solutions repository of 40 problems with written explanations and complexity analysis, plus a tracking sheet of weak topics

tasks.title: Ship a Stripe-integrated full-stack capstone on AWS
tasks.description: Build and deploy a public full-stack app that integrates the Stripe API: user auth, a Stripe payment flow with webhooks handled idempotently, Redis caching and rate limiting, a Dockerized build, a fully automated CI/CD pipeline to AWS, and monitoring dashboards. This is the single artifact that proves every gap is closed.
tasks.deliverable: Public GitHub repo with Dockerfile, CI/CD pipeline, Terraform infrastructure, Redis usage, Stripe webhook handling, tests, and a README containing the live deployed URL

tasks.title: Reposition your resume and tell the transition story
tasks.description: Rewrite your resume to lead with engineering outcomes: frame the Accenture work as building and automating secure cloud infrastructure, quantifying impact (rules audited, incidents resolved, policy changes shipped), and front-load the capstone. Prepare eight STAR stories for behavioral rounds, including one that directly justifies the move from network security into full-stack engineering.
tasks.deliverable: Revised one-page resume, a LinkedIn headline and summary aligned to full-stack engineering, and eight written STAR stories

careerPlans.summary: A 5-phase, roughly 12-17 week plan that converts Dewarsh's deep Azure and network-security operations experience into the full-stack engineering profile Stripe hires for. It closes the five priority gaps — Docker, CI/CD, System Design, AWS, and Redis — with artifacts rather than courses: a containerized environment, a lint-and-test CI pipeline, a Redis idempotency and rate-limiting layer, a hardened multi-stage production image, a staged release pipeline with rollback, an AWS VPC and ECS Fargate deployment, keyless OIDC CI/CD, a payment ledger and idempotency system design, event-driven webhook delivery, a caching and load-testing proof, and a threat model. Phase 3 is deliberately accelerated by mapping existing Azure knowledge (VNet, NSG, UDR, Azure Monitor) directly onto AWS equivalents (VPC, security groups, route tables, CloudWatch), and the capstone in Phase 5 consolidates Docker, CI/CD, AWS, and Redis into one deployable, interview-ready project.

phases.title: Phase 1: Core Fundamentals & Code Quality
phases.description: Close the foundational tooling gap that blocks every later phase. You already write Python/SQL and have deep infrastructure fluency, but there is no evidence of a repeatable app-delivery loop: containerized local dev, tests, and code-quality gates. This phase builds that loop on a single full-stack (TypeScript/Node + Postgres) project that every later task extends, so Docker and CI/CD become muscle memory rather than a tutorial.

tasks.title: Stand Up a Container-First Full Stack App (Node/TypeScript + Postgres)
tasks.description: Scaffold a small but real service: a TypeScript/Express (or Fastify) REST API with Postgres persistence for a domain you know well, e.g. a security-incident tracker with incidents, rules, and change-requests tables. Run it locally today without containers first, then convert the entire dev environment to Docker: a multi-stage Dockerfile (builder -> runtime), a docker-compose.yml bringing up api + Postgres + Redis, named volumes, and an .env contract. This project is the substrate for Phases 2-5, so design it as a repo, not a scratch folder.
tasks.deliverable: GitHub repo with a multi-stage Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml (api + Postgres + Redis), .dockerignore, and a README where `docker compose up` boots the full stack with seeded data.

tasks.title: Install Automated Testing and Code-Quality Gates
tasks.description: Testing and linting are the prerequisites for the CI/CD pipeline in Phase 2 - without them a pipeline only deploys, it does not verify. Add unit tests for domain logic and integration tests that hit the containerized Postgres/Redis, plus strict linting and typing. Cover the paths you will later harden: validation failures, duplicate writes, and DB constraint violations.
tasks.deliverable: Vitest/Jest suite with >=80% line coverage on the service layer, a pg-backed integration test profile, ESLint + Prettier + strict tsconfig, and a pre-commit hook (Husky + lint-staged) that runs lint and tests.

tasks.title: Design the API Contract and Data Model Explicitly
tasks.description: Replace ad-hoc endpoints with a documented contract so later system-design work has a real surface to reason about. Define resources, versioning (/v1), pagination, error envelopes, and status codes. Generate request/response validation from the schema so invalid input is rejected before it reaches the database.
tasks.deliverable: OpenAPI 3.1 spec for the service, runtime request validation wired to it, and a committed ER diagram of the Postgres schema with the migration files that created it.

phases.title: Phase 2: High-Priority Missing Skill Deep Dive
phases.description: Attack the three highest-impact gaps at production depth: Docker beyond `compose up`, a real CI/CD pipeline with gates and environments, and Redis as a cache/coordination layer rather than a key-value toy. Each task hardens the Phase 1 project, so the portfolio grows in quality instead of in sprawl.

tasks.title: Productionize the Docker Image: Size, Security, and Layer Caching
tasks.description: Turn the Phase 1 Dockerfile into something you would ship at a payments company. Split build and runtime stages, run as a non-root user, pin base-image digests, order layers so dependency installs cache independently of source changes, and eliminate build tooling and secrets from the final image. Then defect the image: scan it, generate an SBOM, and measure cold-start and image size before/after.
tasks.deliverable: Distroless/non-root runtime image under 150 MB with pinned digests, a BuildKit cache mount for the package manager, a Trivy scan report (zero HIGH/CRITICAL), and an SBOM generated with Syft.

tasks.title: Build a Multi-Stage CI/CD Pipeline with GitHub Actions
tasks.description: This is your primary missing skill - build the pipeline the way a real platform team would, not a single build job. Create a workflow that gates every PR on lint, typecheck, and tests across an OS/Node matrix, builds and scans the image only after tests pass, publishes to a registry on tags, and deploys to a staging environment behind a manual approval, with dependency caching and concurrency controls so superseded runs cancel.
