Parameterise the Terraform into dev, staging and prod using workspaces or per-environment var-files with environment-specific sizing and scaling floors, stand up a second full environment, and confirm the same pipeline promotes an image between environments with the production approval gate. Run a Cost Explorer and Cost and Usage Report analysis, apply at least three optimisations (rightsize Fargate task CPU/memory, RDS instance class and storage, redis cache sizing versus instance cost, NAT gateway traffic), and document actual dollar deltas. Write and test an RTO/RPO backup-and-restore runbook for RDS and S3, measuring real recovery time.
tasks.deliverable: Multi-environment Terraform (dev/staging/prod) with a fully deployed staging stack promoted to by the pipeline, a cost analysis with three applied optimisations and measured dollar deltas, and a tested RDS/S3 backup-and-restore runbook with the measured RTO.

phases.title: Phase 5: Technical Interview Polish & Review
phases.description: Convert five phases of artifacts into interview performance for a Full Stack Engineer loop. Each deliverable becomes a diagram, a decision and a metric, the system design gap is rehearsed under time pressure, AWS knowledge is consolidated to the point of fluency, and the whole body of work is packaged into one inspectable public repository with a resume that maps to it.

tasks.title: Timed System Design Drills with Whiteboard Diagrams
tasks.description: Convert the Phase 4 documents into verbal fluency. Run at least six timed 35-40 minute prompts solo and two on video or with a peer: a URL shortener, a feed/notification system, a payment service with idempotency, a rate-limited public API, an analytics ingestion pipeline, and a multi-tenant SaaS backend. For each, rehearse the same sequence out loud - clarify requirements and scale, sketch boxes and arrows, choose the data model, place caching and queues, name the bottleneck, name the failure mode - then write the answers you would give to the three hardest follow-ups. Reuse the real artifacts from Phases 2-4 as the source of concrete detail.
tasks.deliverable: Six design-drill packets (requirements, capacity math, diagram, tradeoff decisions, follow-up answers) plus two recorded mock design sessions with a reviewed list of recurring weak points and the fixes for each.

tasks.title: Portfolio Repository, Architecture Writeup and Resume Mapping
tasks.description: Consolidate the code, Dockerfiles, compose files, Terraform, CI/CD workflows, tests, scan reports, SBOM, dashboards and runbooks into one clean public repository whose README reads like an engineering case study: the problem, the architecture diagram, the stack, a `docker compose up` quickstart, an AWS deployment guide with the rollback runbook, observability screenshots, the load-test numbers and the cost analysis. Then write a RESUME.md that maps each project feature to a resume bullet with a metric, and rewrite the experience section so every claim points at something in the repository.
tasks.deliverable: A public GitHub repository with architecture diagram, one-command quickstart, AWS deploy and rollback guides, dashboards and screenshots, load-test and cost numbers, plus a RESUME.md feature-to-bullet mapping and a revised resume section reviewed against the Full Stack Engineer target.

tasks.title: AWS Knowledge Consolidation and Practice Exams
tasks.description: Turn hands-on exposure into exam-grade and interview-grade fluency. Work the core solution-architecture domains - IAM, VPC and networking, ECS/ECR/Fargate, RDS, ElastiCache, S3, SQS, CloudWatch, cost models - and condense each service into a one-page cheat sheet that pairs the service with the exact thing you built with it and the tradeoff you chose. Sit at least three timed practice exams and write a wrong-answer review log that resolves every miss to a service-level explanation rather than a memorised option.
tasks.deliverable: Cheat sheets for 10+ AWS services each linked to a repository artifact, three timed practice-exam score reports, and a wrong-answer review log targeting a consistent 80%+ before scheduling the real exam.

tasks.title: Mock Interviews and a Metrics-Backed STAR Story Bank
tasks.description: Rehearse the full loop and back every story with a number: a live coding round that adds a tested endpoint to the running containerized app, a Docker/AWS/Redis deep dive (multi-stage builds, layer caching, Fargate capacity, security groups, cache eviction and invalidation, connection pooling), a system design round, and behavioural questions. Build a STAR bank of eight or more stories drawn from real Phase 1-4 work with concrete metrics - image size reduced, cache hit rate raised and p95 cut, a container incident diagnosed and root-caused, a deploy automated with OIDC and proven rollback, cost reduced by a measured amount - and log every question asked so the answer can be tightened.
tasks.deliverable: A STAR story bank with 8+ metric-backed stories, two recorded mock interviews (one coding, one system design) with reviewer notes, a question log with revised answers, and a final readiness checklist covering Docker, AWS, Redis, CI/CD and system design.

careerPlans.summary: A 10-week, container-and-cloud-first plan for a candidate targeting Full Stack Engineer at Stripe, sequenced around the three priority gaps (Docker, AWS, Redis) and the two skills that need a level-up (CI/CD, System Design). Phase 1 establishes a runnable, strictly typed, tested full-stack baseline in containers with a first green CI pipeline. Phase 2 goes deep on Docker - hardened images, six-service Compose orchestration, a container incident runbook - and brings Redis in as a real cache-aside layer with a measured hit rate. Phase 3 deploys the containers to AWS entirely as code: least-privilege IAM, VPC, ECS Fargate behind an ALB, RDS, S3, Secrets Manager and ElastiCache, delivered through OIDC with a blue/green deploy and a proven rollback, plus a reusable, scan-gated pipeline. Phase 4 reaches production depth: observability, autoscaling under load to a stated SLO, Redis rate limiting and stampede protection with SQS async workers, three written system design documents grounded in what was actually built, and multi-environment Terraform with cost control and a tested DR runbook. Phase 5 converts it all into interview performance: timed design drills, one public case-study repository with a mapped resume, AWS exam fluency and a metric-backed STAR bank. Every task names the specific gap it closes and ends in an inspectable artifact - no generic filler.

interviewSessions.question: How do you handle graceful degradation and circuit breaking in a distributed microservices architecture?
interviewSessions.answer: Um, so basically we implement the circuit breaker pattern using libraries like Resilience4j or Envoy proxy. When downstream failure rates exceed a 50 percent threshold, the breaker trips to open state, immediately returning cached fallback data or safe default responses instead of cascading timeouts. Like, once health checks pass after a sleep window, it enters half-open state.

voiceTelemetry.deliveryFeedback: Solid flow. Cutting down filler phrases ("um", "like", "basically") will elevate your executive presence.

evaluation.feedback: You correctly named the circuit breaker pattern, real tooling (Resilience4j, Envoy), the open/half-open state machine, a failure-rate threshold, and fallbacks to prevent cascading timeouts — a solid surface-level grasp. However, the answer stays at the pattern-name level and omits the deeper mechanics and trade-offs that separate a strong senior answer: how thresholds actually trigger (minimum call volume, sliding windows), isolation techniques like bulkheads and timeout budgets, fallback consistency and staleness risks, and the broader graceful-degradation toolkit. Tighten the half-open semantics — it probes with limited trial requests after a wait duration, not simply 'health checks passing' — and you would move from recall to real understanding.
strengths: Named the circuit breaker pattern and concrete implementations (Resilience4j, Envoy proxy), showing practical familiarity
Correctly described the three-state lifecycle: closed -> open -> half-open recovery
Captured the core purpose — preventing cascading timeouts by short-circuiting calls to a failing dependency
Mentioned fallbacks (cached data / safe defaults), which is the essence of graceful degradation
missingConcepts: How the trip threshold is computed: minimum number of calls per window, sliding window type (count-based vs time-based), and slow-call rate in addition to failure rate
Bulkhead isolation (separate thread/connection pools per dependency) and per-instance vs shared/distributed breaker state
Timeout and retry discipline — timeouts shorter than the breaker window, bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter to avoid retry storms
Fallback trade-offs: staleness, consistency, and correctness of cached/default responses; degrading to partial results vs failing fast
The broader graceful-degradation toolkit: load shedding, priority-based request dropping, feature flags/kill switches, and read-only degraded modes
Observability (metrics on state transitions, failure and rejection rates) and chaos/failure-injection testing to validate behavior
Distinguishing resilience at the caller vs dependency, and how circuit breaking interacts with load balancing, service mesh, and health checks
evaluation.suggestedImprovement: Strengthen focus on: How the trip threshold is computed: minimum number of calls per window, sliding window type (count-based vs time-based), and slow-call rate in addition to failure rate
evaluation.modelAnswer: In a distributed microservice architecture I treat resilience as layered defenses rather than a single pattern. First, every outbound call gets a strict timeout budget and bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter — retries without backoff are a primary amplifier of outages. Around each remote dependency I wrap a circuit breaker (Resilience4j, Polly, or a service-mesh breaker in Envoy/Istio) that operates on a sliding window, typically time-based, and only trips once a minimum call volume is met (e.g., at least 20 calls in 10s) so a couple of low-traffic errors don't open the breaker prematurely. The breaker is closed by default; when the failure/slow-call rate exceeds a configurable threshold it transitions to open and fails fast for a wait duration instead of piling up threads waiting on timeouts. After the wait it goes half-open and admits a limited number of trial requests; success closes it, failure reopens it. Crucially, I isolate each dependency with a bulkhead — dedicated thread or connection pools — so one degraded service can't consume all capacity, and I apply backpressure/load shedding and priority-based admission when saturation is unavoidable. For graceful degradation, the fallback matters as much as the breaker: I return cached or last-known-good data, computed defaults, or a reduced-fidelity partial response, while being explicit about staleness and correctness trade-offs — sometimes failing fast with a clear error is safer than serving stale data, especially for writes or financial operations. I make degradation dynamic rather than binary using feature flags and kill switches to disable non-critical features (recommendations, analytics) so core flows stay up. Operationally, I instrument state transitions, rejection rates, and fallback usage, alert on the breaker's open events, and validate the whole thing with chaos/failure-injection tests in staging so the fallbacks are exercised before they're needed in production.

voiceTelemetry.deliveryFeedback: Solid flow. Cutting down filler phrases ("um", "like", "basically") will elevate your executive presence.

interviewSessions.question: In React, what triggers a component re-render and how does the reconciliation algorithm work?
interviewSessions.answer: State and prop changes trigger re-renders. React uses the virtual DOM to compute diffs using element keys.

strengths: Identified virtual DOM diffing and state trigger mechanisms accurately.
missingConcepts: Could mention context subscription re-renders and batching.
evaluation.modelAnswer: Component re-renders are triggered by state mutations, prop updates, or context changes...

interviewSessions.question: How do you structure database queries in Node.js to avoid connection exhaustion under load?
interviewSessions.answer: We use a connection pool in PostgreSQL/pg or Mongoose and ensure client.release() or pooled query execution.

strengths: Addressed connection pool management and client release patterns.
missingConcepts: Mentioning statement timeouts, max pool size sizing formula, and queue wait timeouts.
evaluation.modelAnswer: Connection pools manage a fixed set of open sockets...
